meta.title: Rapid Prediction of Exoplanetary Cloud Properties via Autoencoders

abstract: Cloud formation modeling is a crucial frontier for understanding atmospheric composition, dynamics, and the potential habitability (i.e., biosignature) of exoplanets. The formation of cloud particles is determined by local gas temperature, gas density, and gas composition, and hence traces the local thermodynamic conditions. The relevant cloud properties include mean particle size, cloud particle number density, material volume fractions, and depleted element abundances for the elements that participate in the cloud formation process, which are required for solving the radiative transfer. These cloud properties are computed from one-dimensional local pressure-temperature profiles obtained from a three-dimensional general circulation model (GCM). Computing cloud properties involves solving a complex time-dependent reaction-diffusion equation, which is computationally intensive. To reduce these computational costs, we present a neural network (NN) emulator that maps atmospheric parameters to cloud properties via a latent-space representation learned by an autoencoder. By leveraging multiple specialized NN branches for inhomogeneous data, this approach efficiently predicts cloud properties, achieving high accuracy on a GCM grid of 10 hot Jupiters. This generative approach shows high prediction accuracy for cloud properties at lower global temperatures. At higher global temperatures, increased prediction errors are expected, reflecting the greater complexity of cloud formation in these regimes.

blocks.html: The discovery of a wide diversity of extrasolar planets beyond our solar system (exoplanets) is one of modern astronomy’s most profound and evolutionary achievements, from the first confirmed detection in the 1990s [1, 2] to the continuous stream of discoveries that now exceeds 5,000 [3]. Exploring exoplanets has revolutionized our understanding of the universe and reshaped our perceptions of planetary systems. These discoveries have unveiled a breathtaking diversity of exoplanets, ranging from gas giants to rocky worlds, many of which reside in their stars’ habitable zones [4].

We mainly rely on a classical data analysis pipeline comprising several specialized modules: 3D General Circulation Models (GCMs) [5], kinetic cloud formation [6], scattering, and polarization to interpret data from space missions and understand cloud formation phenomena. These tools help characterize atmospheric weather and climate patterns on exoplanets observed by missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) [7], the Characterising ExOPlanet Satellite (CHEOPS) [8], and the PLAnetary Transits and Oscillations of Stars (PLATO) [8].

Building on the successful development of a machine learning (ML) surrogate for GCM data [9], this research focuses on the next critical module: kinetic cloud formation. This phenomenon is mathematically defined by a set of complex partial (reaction-diffusion) equations [10, 11]. However, solving such time-dependent equations is computationally intensive. Therefore, the use of such tools is practically infeasible for the rapid interpretation of observational data from JWST, CHEOPS, and PLATO. To fill this gap, this work focuses on using existing simulated cloud maps data to train a neural network (NN) model that learns this representation and can generate additional cloud maps for unknown grid points with significantly reduced latency. The primary goal is to determine to what extent neural network models can learn these representations, providing a sustainable, high-fidelity alternative to physics-based simulations. Ultimately, we can use NN-predicted cloud maps to interpret observation data from the JWST, CHEOPS, and PLATO space missions in the near future.

The GCM grid [9] is used to train and test the NN model presented in this work, which consists of 10 planets orbiting different host stars, each with a distinct global average temperature Tglobal = 800, 1000, . . . , 3600 K. Each of these virtual 3D exoplanet atmospheres for different host stars from A to M has been sampled by at least 1000 1D local temperature-pressure profiles, for which the cloud properties were consistently calculated using a kinetic, nonequilibrium cloud model. The ML cloud formation dataset contains the relevant cloud properties to radiative transfer: mean particle size (⟨a⟩) [µm], cloud particle mass-to-gas density ratio (ρd/ρ), and material density (ρd)[gcm−3]. For each grid point, we need to train a neural network to learn the relationship between atmospheric variables, such as (Tgas, pgas) profiles, Tglobal, latitude, and longitude, and individual cloud properties, such as ⟨a⟩profiles. blocks.html: It is important to state at the outset that developing a neural network emulator for these cloud maps presents significant challenges due to the highly divergent and nonuniform convergence of profiles across different pressure levels. For instance, mean particle size profiles across various atmospheric samples vary unpredictably, often falling sharply or shifting abruptly at distinct pressure layers, resulting in discontinuous profiles that lack structural similarity even for a specific host star. This absence of a coherent profile representation inherently degrades the performance of conventional neural network emulators, which typically rely on smooth, continuous transitions to learn mapping functions effectively

To create a robust and computationally efficient predictive framework for exoplanetary cloud maps, we propose an architectural design that leverages the dimensionality reduction capabilities of autoencoders coupled with latent (i.e., lower dimensional) space Mapping. This methodology is designed to bypass the traditional, complex time-dependent reaction-diffusion equation. Latent-space regressor architecture: The core idea of the proposed architecture initiates with the treatment of the (Tgas, pgas) profiles. These profiles are high-dimensional, vertically resolved sequences that encapsulate the vertical thermal structure of an atmosphere. Defining a neural network regressor that can map these (Tgas, pgas) profiles in original dimensional space would be challenging due to the increasing dimension. Hence, to process these effectively, we employ an encoder network (the first component of an Autoencoder network) to compress the profile into a low-dimensional latent space (i.e., vector). This latent representation serves purely as a “numerical vector" representing a new, transformed version of the data. Once this latent space is established via a reconstructed (Tgas, pgas) profile, we augment it by concatenating other input parameters, such as the global planetary temperature, latitude, and longitude. This creates a comprehensive Input Latent State that represents a new numerical vector space, capturing the planet’s global spatial context. Simultaneously, we obtain a latent-space representation of the cloud properties (e.g., mean particle size, number density, and volume fractions). Though these properties are highly interdependent, the profile representations are very different; hence, they are projected into a separate output latent space using dedicated autoencoders. By training a set of autoencoders on the cloud data, we ensure that the model learns the “numerical manifold" of physically permissible cloud maps. This is a critical step; rather than forcing the model to predict every individual grid point in the atmosphere, which could lead to disjointed results, we allowed the neural network to predict the underlying latent “representation" of the cloud data.

blocks.caption: The multi-stage machine learning architecture designed to learn from exoplanet cloud maps as described in Sec. 3. “LS" and “OD" stand for latent space and original dimensional space. Schematic representations of cloud properties and (Tgas, pgas) profiles are shown. Because individual profiles from cloud properties differ, independent identical encoder architectures are used to obtain a combined latent space. Individual decoders are used to obtain predictions in the original dimensional space, once the multi-layer perceptron model has been trained to predict the latent-space output from the latent-space input.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: Latent-to-Latent mapping and prediction: The bridge between atmospheric parameters (input ) and cloud properties (output ) is designed through a Deep Dense Neural Network (DNN), often referred to as a “mapping" or “regressor" network. The purpose of this simple neural network architecture is to train the augmented input latent representation and map it directly onto the output latent representation. By operating entirely within these compressed representations, the dense network focuses on the high-level correlations between atmospheric parameters and cloud properties. This specific design for mapping from one latent space to another mimics a generative latent mapping workflow, ensuring that the learned relationships capture the essential, statistically significant features of the training data. Once the DNN predicts an output latent vector, we pass that vector through the pre-trained cloud decoder. The decoder “project" the latent representation back into its original high-dimensional space, providing original cloud properties representation across the entire pressure scale. Figure 1 demonstrates the proposed machine learning workflow of this latent space regressor.

Autoencoder architecture: The Autoencoder class serves as the feature-extraction (i.e., latent-space) engine. It uses a pyramidal structure, shrinking from the input dimension through layers of 512, 256, 128, and 64, down to a compact latent dimension. It has two components, an encoder and a decoder. The role of the encoder is to find the “intrinsic manifold" of the (Tgas, pgas) profiles, distilling vertical grid points into a handful of essential latent variables. The decoder reconstructs the profiles through similar residual stages.

blocks.caption: Training and validation convergence (loss values) of the autoencoder model have been plotted as a function of the number of epochs. The nearly overlapping trajectories of the training (blue) and validation (orange) profiles indicate that the learning process is stable without significant overfitting.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: DNN architecture: Once the (Tgas, pgas) profiles and cloud properties are compressed into their respective latent spaces, this network is trained to bridge them. It takes the Input Latent State, which includes the encoded profile augmented with crucial contextual variables like latitude, longitude, and global temperature, and maps it to the Target Latent State of the cloud properties. The use of LayerNorm and Xavier initialization in this regressor ensures that the diverse scales of spatial coordinates (lat/long) and thermal features are properly balanced during learning.

blocks.caption: Distribution of the RMSE for the reconstructed profiles in a normalized scale (min-max). The histogram compares the training and test sets, showing a high density of profiles with low residual errors. The lower residual error indicates that the autoencoder effectively reconstructs (Tgas, pgas) profiles with minimal deviation from the ground truth from a latent space of dimension 64.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: To evaluate the accuracy of our optimal latent space representation strategy, we conducted a systematic benchmarking of three distinct approaches: Principal Component Analysis (PCA), an AE, and a Variational Autoencoder (VAE). The aim of this exercise is to determine which method could provide the most faithful reconstruction of the 1000-dimensional input profiles while compressing them into a compact, 16-dimensional latent space. We compare the reconstruction error (e.g., RMSE) and the coefficient of determination (R<sup>2</sup>) across these methods (see Figures 4, 5, 6 and Tables 1, 2, 3) and found that the autoencoder-based latent-space representation has lower reconstruction error.

blocks.caption: We compare the predictive performance of PCA and Autoencoder models by examining their RMSE density distributions (y-axis). To visualize these distributions, we utilized kernel density estimation (KDE) plots, which provide a smoothed representation of the error frequency across the dataset. To ensure physical consistency and focus on relevant error ranges, we truncated the distributions to exclude negative values, as RMSE is non-negative by definition.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: To interpret the statistical error measure (RMSE), we examine the relationships among global temperature (T<sup>global</sup>), host star type, and the specific machine learning method used. There is a clear trend: the RMSE increases as global temperature rises. For instance, the RMSE for mean particle size is relatively low at 800 K (0.1098) but increases significantly by 2600 K (0.7510). This implies that the latent-space regressor struggles with more diverse profiles at higher temperatures. This increased complexity in the profiles makes it harder for the models to maintain accuracy. Across all variables (mean particle size, material density, and density ratio), the AE with DNN model consistently achieves the lowest RMSE compared to PCA with DNN and VAE with DNN. This indicates that the AE is the most effective latent-space representation method for this specific cloud modeling dataset. The prediction error also varies with the (A, F, G, K, M)-type host stars. For example, in Table 1, predicting the mean cloud particle size for an M-type star (RMSE 0.8431) is more challenging than for an A-type star (RMSE 0.4973). We conclude that the applied ML methods achieve "good accuracy" in predicting most target cloud profiles. This suggests that, in general, the results are considered satisfactory as a first proof-of-concept.

blocks.html: Capabilities: The “Latent Bridge” model provides nearreal-time inference and consistency when predicting profiles similar to those obtained from expensive physical simulations. Further, it offers an alternative generative model approach to address scalability issues in cloud profile modeling.

Our initial experimental results are promising and indicate that such an ML framework could serve as an NN-based emulator. Furthermore, the comparison between PCA and AE-based latent space representations indicates that the non-linear representation via an autoencoder more effectively captures the complex, higher-order dependencies of the mean-particle profiles than the linear orthogonal projections of PCA, and that it would be considered an optimal scheme for constructing a latent space. Limitations: The proposed “Latent Bridge” model struggles when profiles are highly complex and differ significantly. While effective with similar profile representations, the model struggles to generalize to high-temperature regimes where extreme mixing occurs. The errors at higher global planetary temperatures (Tglobal ≥2000K) are notably higher than those at lower temperatures, which may limit the model’s reliability in hotter planetary environments. Room for Improvements: To make the error “better” (lower), we can adopt several strategies, such as: (a) dividing input profiles into parts based on a pressure (pgas) grid and training separate model blocks, (b) increasing the number of grid points, and (c) testing these architectures for each individual variable without augementing them together in a one latent space.
